title: GeoAI for Ecology
text:
What I Work On
I develop computational methods that combine machine learning, remote sensing, and spatial analysis to study how forests and landscapes change over time — and what that means for biodiversity, carbon storage, and ecosystem health.


🛰️

Remote Sensing & GIS
Leveraging satellite imagery, LiDAR, and geospatial tools to map and monitor forests at scale — from individual tree crowns to continental patterns.
Remote Sensing GIS



🤖

GeoAI & Machine Learning
Applying deep learning, computer vision, and spatial statistics to extract ecological insights from complex geospatial datasets.
Deep Learning Spatial ML



🌳

Forest & Landscape Ecology
Studying how forest structure, composition, and disturbance regimes shape ecosystems across spatial and temporal scales.
Forest Ecology Landscape

title: GeoAI for Ecology
text:
Research Themes

Forest MonitoringSpecies & BiodiversityCarbon & ClimateOpen Tools


Developing automated approaches to detect forest disturbances — including deforestation, degradation, and recovery — using time series of satellite observations. This work combines change detection algorithms with machine learning classifiers to produce timely, accurate maps of forest dynamics.


Using remote sensing and AI to predict species distributions, map biodiversity patterns, and understand how landscape structure influences ecological communities. Multi-sensor data fusion (optical, radar, LiDAR) enables habitat characterization at scales relevant to conservation planning.


Quantifying forest carbon stocks and fluxes through integration of field measurements, allometric models, and remotely sensed canopy structure. These methods support national forest inventories, REDD+ monitoring, and climate change mitigation strategies.


Building open-source software that makes geospatial ecology research more reproducible and accessible. Current projects include forestPulse, an R package taking forest field plots and drone or satellite imagery through to analysis-ready summaries and iLand model inputs, and iLAND Workbench, a QGIS plugin for individual-based forest landscape and disturbance modeling with full data-preparation workflows, runtime management, and reproducible analysis pipelines. Together they form a single pipeline from field data to simulation.

title: Research
text:
My research sits at the intersection of geospatial artificial intelligence and ecology, developing computational methods to understand how forests and landscapes change and what those changes mean for the planet.




🛰️


Automated detection of deforestation, degradation, and recovery using satellite time series and machine learning classifiers. Dense Landsat and Sentinel-2 stacks are used to pinpoint both the timing and the magnitude of change, so that gradual degradation is separated from abrupt clearing.
Change Detection Landsat Sentinel



🌍


Modeling how landscape structure and fragmentation affect species movement, gene flow, and ecosystem resilience. Graph-theoretic and circuit-based approaches turn land cover maps into networks whose weak links reveal conservation priorities.
Connectivity Graph Theory



📊


Developing geospatial machine learning models for ecological prediction, including species distribution models and above-ground biomass estimation. Emphasis is on spatially aware validation, so that reported accuracy survives contact with new landscapes.
GeoAI Prediction



🌿


Using multi-sensor remote sensing to characterize habitats and predict biodiversity patterns across spatial scales. Fusing optical, radar, and LiDAR data captures both the composition and the three-dimensional structure that species respond to.
Biodiversity LiDAR








Open by defaultFreely available dataBuilt for practitioners


Code, data, and methods are released openly wherever licensing allows. Analyses are built as reproducible pipelines rather than one-off scripts, so results can be re-run, checked, and extended by others.


The methods here are designed around openly licensed Earth observation data — Landsat, Sentinel, SoilGrids, LANDFIRE, ESA WorldCover — so that they remain usable by researchers and practitioners without commercial imagery budgets.


Research outputs are packaged as tools people can actually run: QGIS plugins, R packages, and documented workflows, rather than results that stop at the figure in a paper.












forestPulse: Analyse Forest Structure and Disturbance from Field and Remote Sensing Data

Paudel, S. (2025). Zenodo. Version 0.3.0. R package, MIT licensed.


DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.17887640 Code Docs

Paudel, S. (2026). Zenodo. Version 4.1.0.


DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19300115 Code Docs






Peer-reviewed articles will be listed here as they appear. In the meantime, the most current list is on Google Scholar.






Analysis code and, where licensing permits, derived datasets accompanying this research are published openly on GitHub, alongside The CEDAR Lab organization. Software releases are archived on Zenodo so they can be cited with a persistent DOI.


I’m always open to collaborations at the intersection of GeoAI and ecology — joint analyses, method development, student co-supervision, or applying these tools to your study system.

title: Tools & Packages
text:
Open-source software is central to reproducible ecological research. Here are the tools I develop and maintain.





A dockable QGIS plugin that brings the iLAND individual-based forest landscape and disturbance model into a GIS workflow. It provides runtime management, module exploration, data-preparation pipelines for climate, soil, and stand-grid inputs, and reproducible analysis workflows — all from within QGIS.



DOI


GitHub Repository QGIS Plugin Repository


OverviewInstallationCitation


iLAND Workbench bridges the gap between the iLAND simulation model and the QGIS ecosystem, making forest landscape modeling accessible without leaving your GIS environment. Key capabilities include:

Runtime management with automatic download and verification of iLANDc across Windows, macOS, and Linux
Module and submodule exploration directly from the iLAND source tree
Complete climate workflows: future climate download, historical data, and conversion/validation pipelines
Soil data acquisition from SSURGO and SoilGrids
Stand-grid source workflows via LANDFIRE EVT and ESA WorldCover
Landscape pre-flight validation before model creation
Interactive SQLite plot browser for inspecting exported iLand output databases
Full QGIS Processing provider integration



# Requires QGIS Desktop 3.28 or newer
# In QGIS: Plugins → Manage and Install Plugins → Install from ZIP
# Download iland_qgis_plugin.zip from the GitHub Releases page
The plugin ships as a small, runtime-free package. The native iLAND console runtime (iLANDc) needed to run simulations is acquired automatically on first use.


@software{paudel2026iland,
  author    = {Paudel, Sushil},
  title     = {{iLAND Workbench: QGIS-based iLAND Workbench for
                hassle-free installation and reproducible analysis
                workflows}},
  year      = {2026},
  version   = {4.1.0},
  publisher = {Zenodo},
  doi       = {10.5281/zenodo.19300115},
  url       = {https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19300115}
}









forestPulse turns forest field plots and drone or satellite imagery into analysis-ready summaries, and assembles the spatial and tabular inputs needed to drive the iLand forest landscape model. Current release v0.3.0, MIT licensed.



DOI


GitHub Repository Releases Report an Issue

Together with iLAND Workbench, forestPulse completes the pipeline: it prepares the landscape, climate, and tree-initialisation inputs, and the plugin runs the simulation inside QGIS.

OverviewInstallationQuick startFunction referenceCitation


The package covers two connected areas, aimed at researchers, ecologists, and forest managers moving from field plots and imagery through to process-based modeling.
Field and remote-sensing analysis

Index geotagged raster imagery into a spatial catalogue and match it to field plots
Compute canopy height models (CHM), classify canopy gaps, and derive per-plot gap geometry
Calculate 37 RGB-derived vegetation indices from drone orthomosaics
Locate individual trees from compass bearings and distance measurements
Summarise plot-level basal area, crown density, and species composition
Standardise messy species names and audit what changed

iLand model inputs

Impute field plots to pixels with modified random-forest imputation to build wall-to-wall tree lists, flagging poorly matched pixels
Derive daily climate variables — vapour pressure deficit, radiation — from gridMET following the FAO-56 approach, and write a per-cluster SQLite climate database in iLand’s exact format
Build the stand grid, resource-unit environment grid and file, and the tree-initialisation file, then cross-validate them — step by step or through a single build_iland_landscape() call



# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("paudelsushil/forestPulse")
Requires R 4.1.0 or newer. Some capabilities use optional packages declared in Suggests: install RSQLite for climate databases, yaImpute for plot-to-pixel imputation, and future/future.apply for parallel spatial sampling.


Field and remote-sensing analysis:
library(forestPulse)

# 1. Build a spatial catalogue of geotagged rasters and match it to field plots
catalog      <- build_catalog(input = "path/to/imagery", output = "catalog.geojson")
plots        <- sf::read_sf("plots.shp")
plot_imagery <- match_imagery(catalog, plots)

# 2. Canopy height model, then per-plot canopy gap metrics
chm     <- compute_chm("dsm.tif", "dtm.tif", output = "chm.tif")
metrics <- extract_plot_metrics(chm = chm, plots = plots,
                                radius = 15.24, gap_threshold = 3)

# 3. An RGB vegetation index and a plot-level basal-area summary
vegetation_index("ExG", image_path = "orthomosaic.tif")
calculate_basal_area(tree_table, summary = "plot")
Preparing inputs for the iLand model:
# Daily climate from a gridMET extraction -> per-cluster SQLite climate database
clim <- gridmet_preprocessing(
  data        = gridmet_daily,   # one row per cluster-day
  cluster_col = "cluster",
  date_col    = "date",
  temp_unit   = "K",
  vpd_source  = "compute"        # derive VPD from temperature + humidity
)
write_iland_climate(clim, "database/climate.sqlite", split_col = "cluster")

# Stand grid + wall-to-wall tree initialisation via plot-to-pixel imputation
stand_grid <- create_stand_grid(stands, id_field = "stand_id",
                                filename = "gis/stand_grid.asc")
target     <- make_target_from_rasters(predictor_stack, stand_grid)
pixel_plot <- impute_plots_to_pixels(reference, target, predictors, responses)
build_iland_init(pixel_plot, tree_lists, out_path = "init/init_trees.txt")









Topic
Functions




Raster catalogue
build_catalog(), read_catalog(), query_catalog(), match_imagery(), footprint()


Canopy height & gaps
compute_chm(), classify_gaps(), gap_metrics(), extract_plot_metrics()


Vegetation indices
vegetation_index() — 37 RGB indices


Tree location
locate_tree()


Basal area & summaries
calculate_basal_area(), calculate_species_basal_area(), calculate_plot_species_basal_area(), calculate_plot_summary()


Crown density
calculate_crownDensity(), show_calculation_details(), plot_summary()


Species standardisation
clean_species_names(), get_species_mapping(), check_unmapped_species(), compare_species_changes()


Climate (iLand)
gridmet_preprocessing(), calc_vpd(), calc_saturation_vapor_pressure(), convert_radiation(), write_iland_climate()


Landscape (iLand)
create_stand_grid(), create_environment_grid(), create_environment_file(), build_iland_landscape(), validate_landscape()


Imputation & init
impute_plots_to_pixels(), make_target_from_rasters(), flag_far_imputations(), build_iland_init(), create_init_file()



Full documentation is available in the package help pages (?forestPulse) and the repository README.

title: The CEDAR Lab
text:
The CEDAR Lab builds computational methods and open-source software for understanding how forests and landscapes change — combining machine learning, satellite remote sensing, and spatial analysis to answer questions that matter for conservation, carbon, and biodiversity.
The CEDAR Lab on GitHub Our research



Computational Ecology, Data Analytics, and Remote sensing — the three strands that run through everything the lab does.


🧮


Turning ecological questions into models that can be run, tested, and re-run. Simulation of forest dynamics and disturbance sits alongside statistical inference from field and satellite observation.
Modeling Simulation



📊


Machine learning and spatial statistics applied to large, messy environmental datasets — with an emphasis on validation that holds up when a model meets a landscape it has never seen.
Machine Learning Spatial Stats



🛰️


Openly licensed Earth observation — Landsat, Sentinel, LiDAR, radar — used to measure forest structure, composition, and change from the individual crown to the continental scale.
Earth Observation LiDAR








Open by defaultFree and open dataTools, not just papersTeaching in the open


Code, methods, and — where licensing allows — data are released publicly. Software is archived on Zenodo so it carries a citable DOI, and analyses are built as reproducible pipelines rather than one-off scripts that only run on one machine.


The lab deliberately builds on openly licensed Earth observation and environmental data: Landsat, Sentinel, SoilGrids, LANDFIRE, and ESA WorldCover. Methods that depend on commercial imagery budgets are methods most of the world cannot use.


Research outputs are packaged so other people can actually run them — QGIS plugins, R packages, documented workflows. A result that stops at a figure in a paper is only half finished.


Methods are explained publicly through written tutorials and the GeoAI for Ecology YouTube channel, so that researchers without a computational background can pick these tools up.











Founder · PhD Researcher
Sushil founded The CEDAR Lab to advance open, reproducible research in geospatial ecology. His work combines machine learning, remote sensing, and spatial analysis to study forest and landscape dynamics, and he develops the lab’s open-source tools.

title: The CEDAR Lab
text:
Computational Ecology, Data Analytics, and Remote sensing — the three strands that run through everything the lab does.


🧮


Turning ecological questions into models that can be run, tested, and re-run. Simulation of forest dynamics and disturbance sits alongside statistical inference from field and satellite observation.
Modeling Simulation



📊


Machine learning and spatial statistics applied to large, messy environmental datasets — with an emphasis on validation that holds up when a model meets a landscape it has never seen.
Machine Learning Spatial Stats



🛰️


Openly licensed Earth observation — Landsat, Sentinel, LiDAR, radar — used to measure forest structure, composition, and change from the individual crown to the continental scale.
Earth Observation LiDAR

title: The CEDAR Lab
text:
Open by defaultFree and open dataTools, not just papersTeaching in the open


Code, methods, and — where licensing allows — data are released publicly. Software is archived on Zenodo so it carries a citable DOI, and analyses are built as reproducible pipelines rather than one-off scripts that only run on one machine.


The lab deliberately builds on openly licensed Earth observation and environmental data: Landsat, Sentinel, SoilGrids, LANDFIRE, and ESA WorldCover. Methods that depend on commercial imagery budgets are methods most of the world cannot use.


Research outputs are packaged so other people can actually run them — QGIS plugins, R packages, documented workflows. A result that stops at a figure in a paper is only half finished.


Methods are explained publicly through written tutorials and the GeoAI for Ecology YouTube channel, so that researchers without a computational background can pick these tools up.

title: About
text:
PhD Researcher · Founder, The CEDAR Lab
I’m a researcher working at the intersection of geospatial artificial intelligence and ecology. My work combines machine learning, remote sensing, and spatial analysis to study forest and landscape dynamics — understanding how ecosystems change and what we can do about it.
I founded The CEDAR Lab (Computational Ecology, Data Analytics & Remote Sensing) to advance open, reproducible research in geospatial ecology, and I run the GeoAI for Ecology YouTube channel to make these methods accessible to a wider audience.

🐙 GitHub 🏛️ The CEDAR Lab 🎥 YouTube 📡 Blog RSS 






My research draws on forest ecology, landscape ecology, geospatial data science, and AI. I’m particularly interested in how we can use freely available satellite data and modern machine learning to answer ecological questions that matter for conservation and land management.
I believe in open science — the tools we build, the code we write, and the knowledge we generate should be accessible to everyone. Everything on this site, from the software to the tutorials, is released openly so that others can use, check, and build on it.






🌲


Making the iLAND simulation model usable from within QGIS, so that forest and disturbance modeling doesn’t require leaving your GIS environment.
iLAND Workbench



📦


Building forestPulse to take forest field plots and drone imagery through to analysis-ready summaries and iLand model inputs.
forestPulse



🎓


Producing video tutorials and written guides on remote sensing, GIS, and geospatial AI for ecologists getting started with these methods.
GeoAI for Ecology on YouTube







I’m always open to collaborations, speaking invitations, and questions about the research or the tools. Drop me a message and I’ll get back to you.
